pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9-11 (Upper KS2/Grades 4-6): threats to insects and conservation — populations are declining worldwide; causes include habitat loss, pesticides, light pollution (disrupting nocturnal insects) and climate change. Pollinator decline threatens our food. What children can DO: plant pollinator-friendly gardens, cut pesticide use, join citizen science (e.g. the Big Butterfly Count).
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 Y4 (environments can change and pose dangers to living things) and Y6 (human impact / interdependence); working-scientifically (evidence, citizen science data).
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-LS4-4 (solutions to a problem caused by environmental change) and 5-ESS3-1 / MS-LS2-5 (human impact and protecting biodiversity/ecosystem services).
• Operational details — builds directly on the ecosystem-roles node: because insects do so much, their decline matters. Two halves: (a) understand the DRIVERS with evidence (link each threat to a mechanism — pesticides kill non-targets, light traps night-fliers, habitat loss removes food/shelter), and (b) AGENCY — concrete, realistic actions children can take, framed as efficacy not doom. Citizen science connects them to real data-gathering. Keep it evidence-based and avoid catastrophising.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): names three threats to insects. Tier B (age 10): explains why declining pollinators are a problem for our food. Tier C (age 11): links a specific threat to its mechanism and proposes two realistic conservation actions (and how citizen science helps).
bestPractices: Link each threat to a concrete mechanism (pesticides kill non-target insects; light lures night-fliers; habitat loss removes food/shelter).
Balance problem with AGENCY — give realistic, concrete actions and frame them as effective, not futile.
Keep it evidence-based and avoid catastrophising, which can disengage children.
Connect to real citizen science (e.g. butterfly counts) so children see how data reveals trends and how they can contribute.
Build on insects' ecosystem roles — decline matters BECAUSE of what insects do.
keyRepresentations: A neighbourhood with a live insect-population meter and threat toggles.
An action/design mode (wildflower strip, log pile, shielded lights).
A citizen-science counting task showing a trend over time.
commonMisconceptions: 'Fewer insects would be a good thing' — ignores their essential roles and the knock-on harm.
'Insect decline has no clear cause' — the drivers are known and specific.
'Nothing an individual does can help' — local action measurably supports insect populations.
'All pesticides only kill the target pest' — many harm beneficial insects too.
'Climate change doesn't affect tiny insects' — it shifts ranges, timing and survival.

learn.summary: For ages 9-11 (Upper KS2 / Grades 4-6): why insect populations are declining and what children can realistically do about it. The teaching has two linked halves: (a) understanding the DRIVERS and tying each to a concrete mechanism (pesticides kill non-target insects like bees; streetlights lure and trap night-fliers such as moths; habitat loss removes food and shelter; climate change shifts ranges, timing and survival), and (b) AGENCY — proposing realistic, cause-matched conservation actions framed as effective rather than futile. The discriminating idea, carried forward from insects' ecosystem roles, is WHY the decline harms people: pollinator loss means less fruit and vegetables, and fewer insects means less food for birds and other wildlife and less nutrient recycling. Keep it evidence-based and avoid catastrophising.

activities.title: Toggle the threats, then redesign for recovery
feedback: If a learner treats decline as causeless, revisit each toggle and ask them to name the mechanism aloud (e.g. 'light disrupts night insects like moths').

If an action is chosen without matching it to a threat, ask: 'Which threat does a wildflower strip fix, and which does it leave untouched?' (wildflowers add food/shelter but do not fix light pollution).
If a learner expects one action to solve everything, note that different threats need different fixes and that scale matters — see the collective-action discussion in the conversation activity.
activities.rationale: Turning both harm and remedy into levers the learner controls is intended to make the drivers and the efficacy of action reasoned rather than merely asserted; matching each action to a specific cause builds the integrated cause→consequence reasoning the topic targets. An optional live population indicator that rises and falls as toggles and actions change makes the mechanism concrete, but the core requirement is that the learner state mechanisms and match actions to causes — the indicator is a scaffold, not the lesson.
sourceClaims: Insect declines are driven by habitat loss, pesticide use, light pollution and climate change; pollinator loss threatens food production; citizen-science schemes like the Big Butterfly Count gather trend data.
Students generate and compare solutions to a problem caused by environmental change affecting organisms (3-LS4-4) and consider human impacts on biodiversity/ecosystems (5-ESS3-1, MS-LS2-5).
learnerActions: Starting from a healthy neighbourhood scene with an 'insect health' indicator, turn on one threat at a time and observe the stated mechanism: a bright streetlight lures moths to circle uselessly all night; a pesticide spray drifts and kills bees along with the target pests; paving over a meadow erases food and shelter.
After each threat, state in your own words WHY it lowers insect numbers (the mechanism), not just that numbers fall.
Switch to an action/design mode and intervene: sow a wildflower strip, build a log pile, shield or dim the lights, swap spraying for natural predators like ladybirds.
For each action you choose, say which specific threat it addresses — and name a threat it does NOT fix.
Explain why the population responds to your choices, so efficacy is reasoned, not just observed.
activities.intendedInsight: Insect decline is not mysterious: it has specific, identifiable causes with clear mechanisms, and concrete local actions can help when matched to the right cause.

activities.title: Count butterflies over several visits
feedback: If a learner judges the population from one count, ask what a single low count could be caused by (weather, time of day) and why repeating helps.
If a learner sees their own count as meaningless, explain that many people's counts combine into a dataset large enough to show national trends.
activities.rationale: Working scientifically with repeated observation and trend-reading is part of the standards, and connecting to a real scheme shows how evidence of decline is actually gathered and how individual contributions scale.
sourceClaims: Insect declines are driven by habitat loss, pesticide use, light pollution and climate change; pollinator loss threatens food production; citizen-science schemes like the Big Butterfly Count gather trend data.
learnerActions: Carry out a simple repeated 'count' of butterflies (or another insect) over several visits, keeping conditions as similar as possible (same place, same length of count, similar time of day, warm dry weather), and record each count.

Compare the counts and describe what they show (rising, falling, steady), remembering that a few visits in one year show short-term change caused by things like weather and season, not a long-term population trend.

Explain why repeating the count matters: a single count can mislead, repeated counts under similar conditions give a more reliable picture, and long-term trends come from comparing the same time of year across many years and many sites.
Connect this to real citizen-science schemes such as the Big Butterfly Count and describe how data from many people reveals large-scale changes scientists can act on.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated, standardised observations pooled from many people over many years turn single snapshots into evidence of trends, and ordinary people (including children) can contribute real data that scientists use.

activities.title: Ask a conservation scientist about your own situation
feedback: If a learner says nothing can be done, prompt them to recall how, in the simulation, actions matched to a threat raised the insect indicator, explain that real habitat improvements can help local insects, and ask them to name one action fitting their own space.
If a learner proposes an action that doesn't fit their situation, help them adapt it (balcony pots of pollinator-friendly plants rather than a meadow).
activities.rationale: A responsive dialogue can address a learner's specific circumstances and reasoning in a way a fixed scenario cannot, and is intended to counter the 'nothing I do helps' fatalism. This is a complementary mode, not a replacement for the hands-on mechanism and action work; its efficacy relative to other formats is not established by the sources.
learnerActions: Pose an open, specific question to an in-role conservation scientist or entomologist, e.g. 'We only have a small balcony — what could I realistically do?'
Explain your reasoning about causes and actions so the expert can probe and extend it.
Respond when the expert gently challenges fatalism ('Is it hopeless?') by giving reasons that local action can contribute.
activities.intendedInsight: Conservation involves values and open, situation-specific decisions; realistic action exists even in constrained circumstances, and realistic local action can contribute, so defeatism is not the only reasonable response.

activities.title: Match threats to mechanisms and sort helpful from harmful actions
feedback: For a mismatched threat-mechanism pair, restate the mechanism and ask the learner to re-pair it.
If 'keep insects as pets indoors' is marked helpful, explain that this does not address habitat, pesticides or light and does not support wild populations.
If the food link is weak, bridge via pollination: fewer pollinators → less fruit and vegetables.
activities.rationale: Checks for knowledge and action-choices complement the construction tasks. Matching and sorting can verify classification of threats and actions but do not by themselves require the learner to independently construct and justify the cause→consequence→action chain, so pair them with the explanation and design activities. The decline-drivers claim is cited only to support the pollinator→food content being checked, not a comparative claim about task formats.
sourceClaims: Insect declines are driven by habitat loss, pesticide use, light pollution and climate change; pollinator loss threatens food production; citizen-science schemes like the Big Butterfly Count gather trend data.
learnerActions: Match each threat to its effect (e.g. light → trapped/disoriented moths; spray → dead bees; paving → lost food and shelter).
Sort proposed responses into genuinely helpful versus unhelpful or misdirected (e.g. planting wildflowers and reducing spray vs keeping wild insects as pets indoors).
Answer why declining pollinators matter for the food we eat, choosing and justifying the reason rather than only recognising it.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall that threats map to specific mechanisms, that helpful actions target habitat/pesticides/light at scale, and that pollinator loss has a direct food consequence.

activities.title: Explore a before/after habitat and explain the links
feedback: If a learner only labels features, ask them to explain the consequence of each (why does losing the meadow reduce insects?).
Prompt them to state what would most improve the degraded scene and why.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal habitat scene informs and supports prediction and explanation. Because it does not simulate the population's response to the learner's own intervention, it works best as a scaffold toward the interactive toggle/redesign activity rather than a substitute for it; this is a narrow affordance of that specific format, not a claim that static images cannot teach.
sourceClaims: KS2 pupils learn that environments can change and this can pose dangers to living things (Y4) and study human impact and interdependence (Y6).
learnerActions: Examine a split scene of a healthy versus degraded habitat and reveal the threats and actions present in each.
For each revealed threat, state its mechanism and predict its effect on insects.
For each revealed action, say which threat it counters.
Explain why the degraded side supports fewer insects, connecting to food webs and pollination.
activities.intendedInsight: A habitat's condition is the sum of specific threats and actions, each with a traceable effect on insect populations.

constraints: Keep the framing evidence-based and avoid catastrophising; doom-laden framing can disengage children. Balance the problem with realistic, achievable actions presented as effective.

Each threat must be tied to a concrete mechanism, not left as a bare list (pesticides kill non-target insects; light lures/disrupts night-fliers; habitat loss removes food and shelter; climate change shifts ranges/timing/survival).
Build on insects' ecosystem roles: the decline matters BECAUSE of what insects do (pollination → food; prey → birds and wildlife; nutrient recycling).

Frame individual actions honestly: a single garden is part of a larger collective effort, not a total fix for a global problem. Avoid implying one action solves everything, and avoid the goal of preventing ALL insect deaths.

Recognition, matching and sorting tasks verify knowledge and choices; they do not by themselves require the learner to independently construct the cause→consequence→action explanation. Pair them with activities that demand that construction.

Before/after reveal scenes and conversation modes are complements to hands-on cause-and-action work, each with different affordances; none is presented as the only way to teach the topic, and no format is asserted as more effective than another.
Address the misconception that fewer insects is good by weighing the few nuisance species against the many essential ones and their services.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The three listed sources are marked verified:false in the row (DfE KS2 programmes of study; NGSS 3-LS4-4 / 5-ESS3-1 / MS-LS2-5; Butterfly Conservation / IPBES / insect-decline reviews). Standards citations and the general decline-drivers claim should be confirmed against primary documents before relying on them.

The legacy row rated 3D interactive 'poor' because it 'adds no conceptual value'; this universal dismissal has been dropped. 3D was simply not developed here as the concept is driver-and-action reasoning on a population rather than spatial exploration — no claim is made that 3D could never contribute.

The source's claim that a fixed scene 'can't run the population response' is retained only as a narrowly scoped affordance note (it does not simulate the learner's own intervention), not as a claim that fixed images cannot teach.

No comparative efficacy between the interactive model, conversation, quiz and reveal-image formats is established by the sources; the row's 'ideal/strong/possible' rankings are not asserted as evidence of effectiveness.

The recognition/sorting-vs-construction point and the 'dialogue addresses specific circumstances' point are agent pedagogical reasoning about task affordances, not source-verified efficacy; wording kept as intended/may rather than proven.

The row frames local action as 'effective'/that it 'measurably' helps; this anti-fatalism framing is preserved in qualified form, but its efficacy is not established by the verified:false sources and should be confirmed before being presented as settled evidence.

probeDeeper: 'You said fewer bites sounds good. What do bees and other pollinators do for the food on your plate — so what happens if they decline?'
'Light pollution mainly affects moths and other night insects. Why would streetlights be a threat to them?' (specific cause → mechanism)
'If your family planted wildflowers, which threat does that fix — and which threats does it NOT fix?' (forces matching action to cause)
'Would one family's garden be enough to reverse the decline? Why do lots of people need to act?'
assess.correctAnswer: Disagree — falling insect numbers are a serious problem, not good news. Causes include habitat loss (fewer wild places to live), pesticides (which poison insects), light pollution (which disrupts night insects like moths), and climate change. It matters for people because so much of our food depends on pollinating insects — fewer pollinators means less fruit and vegetables — and because insects feed birds and other wildlife and recycle nutrients. A family could help by planting wildflowers/pollinator-friendly plants, cutting pesticide use, leaving wild patches, turning off unnecessary lights, or joining a citizen-science count like the Big Butterfly Count.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sees insects as pests — thinks fewer insects is a good thing, not a problem
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reconnect decline to services they value: fewer pollinators → less fruit; fewer insects → hungry birds. Weigh a few nuisance species against the many essential ones before judging the decline good.
errorPatterns.distractor: Agree — fewer insects means fewer bites and stings, so it's good for us
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Agrees the decline is good (fewer bites/stings); no sense of loss

errorPatterns.pattern: Lists threats and actions but can't explain WHY the decline harms humans — facts without the causal link to food/ecosystems
errorPatterns.nextMove: Bridge with the roles from the previous topic: pollinators → our food; food source → birds/wildlife. Make each threat's consequence explicit rather than a standalone list.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: names habitat loss/pesticides and 'plant flowers' but can't say why it matters to people

errorPatterns.pattern: Suggests unrealistic or misdirected 'help' — e.g. keeping insects as pets indoors, or thinks one garden fixes a global problem, or that we should stop ALL insects dying
errorPatterns.nextMove: Steer toward habitat- and pesticide-focused, scalable actions (wildflowers, less spray, wild patches, citizen science). Frame small actions as part of a bigger collective effort, not a total fix.
errorPatterns.distractor: The best way to help is to catch insects and keep them safe indoors as pets
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Proposes actions that don't address habitat/pesticides/light, or over-claims that a single action solves it

responseLevels.gap: Welcomes the decline as good, or can't name any cause; sees no problem for people.
responseLevels.full: Explains the decline is a problem, links causes (habitat loss, pesticides, light pollution, climate) to consequences for food and wildlife via insects' roles, AND proposes a realistic, cause-matched action — integrated reasoning across the domain, not a memorised list.
responseLevels.partial: Names threats and a helpful action but as disconnected facts — can't explain WHY declining insects harm people (misses the pollination/food and food-web links), or matches actions loosely to causes.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Scientists say insect numbers are falling fast around the world. A child says: 'Fewer insects just means fewer bites and stings — that's good for us, isn't it?' Do you agree? Explain what's causing the decline, why it's actually a problem for people, and one thing a family could do to help.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has integrated the domain links the CAUSES to the consequences via insects' ecological ROLES (pollination → food; food source → wildlife) and offers a realistic action. A child who still sees insects as pests welcomes the decline, or lists causes and actions as disconnected facts without explaining WHY fewer insects harms people. The second tier ('why is it a problem for people?') is the discriminator: it requires carrying forward the ecosystem-roles idea, not just naming threats.
